questions.question: Explain how a tender board differs from a class audience, list the rubric headings for this tender and how they shape the use of time, and state what earns a board's confidence.
questions.expected_answer: A tender board represents the client and is judged by whether the headgear it chooses is built on time, within budget and safely, so it looks for risk as well as excellence, has read or expects the bid documents, uses the presentation to test their claims through the demonstration and questions, often includes specialists who ask from their own knowledge, and compares several companies against one set of criteria while scoring. The rubric headings are understanding of the problem, from the brief and investigation; technical design, from the gear calculations, systems diagram and working drawing; model performance against specifications, from the demonstration and evaluation table; construction method, from the flow chart and making record; budget completeness and realism; social and environmental responsibility, from the impact report and its link to the design; and the presentation's clarity, teamwork and question handling, with time allocated in proportion to marks. Confidence is earned by evidence over claims, numbers over adjectives and candour over polish, such as stating the ratio, the measured lift time, the load at which the model stalled and the costed fix, and by visible teamwork under pressure.

questions.question: Set out the six documents that form the spine of the bid presentation, describe how seven minutes is divided among them, and explain how presenting roles are allocated and the presentation rehearsed.
questions.expected_answer: The documents are the investigation record; the brief with specifications; the drawings, including the gear drawing, systems diagram and working drawing; the flow chart with the making record; the model with its evaluation table; and the budget with the impact report alongside. About one minute introduces the company and the problem from the brief with investigation facts and shows the model; one minute presents the design from the working drawing, the chosen form, the rejected ideas and key specifications; one minute presents the mechanism from the gear drawing and systems diagram with input speed, ratio and stages, output and lift speed, direction and mechanical advantage; two minutes are the demonstration with results narrated against the evaluation table; one minute covers the construction method, what changed in the build, the budget total, largest items, contingency and sources, and the impact report's finding and design response; and thirty seconds give conclusions, recommendations and the invitation for questions. Each member presents the part they did and holds that document, the budget is presented by its compiler, handovers are planned, notes are on cards, and the whole is rehearsed twice with a timer, once before another company posing hard questions, and cut to time so the demonstration is never squeezed.

questions.question: Describe how the live demonstration is prepared and run, how specialist, budget and impact questions are answered, and how the board reaches and communicates its decision.
questions.expected_answer: Before the session the model is tested on the actual presentation table with the shaft drop clamped in place, fresh batteries, the string wound correctly, the cage loaded and weighed, and the brake and bumper checked, with a checklist on the base ticked before standing. During the demonstration one member operates the switch and brake, one narrates against the evaluation table, one times and measures sway, and one watches the board; the sequence shows the empty cage, states the load, times the lift aloud, holds with the brake at mid-shaft, shows the bumper at the top, measures sway with the 1 kilogram on the platform, swings the cage for the topple test and lowers under power, and any live failure is reported with the earlier recorded result rather than hidden. Specialist questions are answered with the method and measured evidence rather than guesses; budget questions are answered with the source and date of each rate, the method of each estimate, and honest acknowledgement of any omission with its likely cost; impact questions are answered with what the design actually does; the member who did the work answers, and an unknown is met with how the team would find out and noted for the portfolio. The board scores each company against the rubric during and after the presentations, confers, and announces the award with reasons covering specifications met, budget credibility, question handling and each company's strengths and improvements, which the companies record as the project's final evaluation.
